summary: Analyzes whether the newer stateful IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanisms avoid the problems that led the IETF to deprecate NAT-PT. It is informational.

eli5.summary: An old translator was fired for making mistakes. This checks whether the new translators repeat the same mistakes.

questions: is stateful nat64 better than nat-pt
what problems can stateful translation not solve
subtitle: Assessing improvements in IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanisms.

tldr.problem: NAT-PT, an IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanism, was deprecated due to fundamental problems. The question is whether newer stateful translation mechanisms fix these issues.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyzes stateful NAT64 against each problem identified in RFC 4966, categorizing them as impossible to solve, solvable with workarounds, or solved.
tldr.outcome: NAT64 solves some problems but leaves others unaddressed. Many of the remaining issues are inherent to all NAT-based solutions, not specific to NAT64.

today: RFC 6889 is an Informational document published in April 2013. It has not been obsoleted. Stateful 64 (NAT64) remains in use for IPv6-to-IPv4 translation in many deployments, though with the limitations identified in this analysis. The document is regularly referenced when evaluating the appropriateness of NAT64 for specific deployment scenarios.

sections.title: The Translation Problem
sections.content:
The Internet is transitioning from IPv4 (the older address system) to IPv6 (the new one). During this transition, IPv6-only networks sometimes need to communicate with IPv4-only networks. NAT-PT (Network Address Translation - Protocol Translation) was an early attempt to bridge this gap by translating addresses and protocols between the two systems. However, the IETF deprecated it due to serious technical problems documented in RFC 4966.

In response, a new set of mechanisms called stateful 64 translation (or NAT64) was developed as a replacement. This document analyzes whether stateful 64 avoids the problems that doomed NAT-PT. The mechanisms analyzed include RFC 6145 (translation algorithm), RFC 6146 (stateful NAT64), RFC 6147 (DNS64), RFC 6052 (IPv6 addressing of translators), and RFC 6144 (translation framework).
sections.eli5: When networks speak different languages, you need a translator. IPv4 and IPv6 are different languages for the internet. NAT-PT was a translator that broke, so engineers made a new one and asked: does the new one work better?

sections.title: Why Stateful 64 is Different
sections.content:
A key innovation in stateful 64 is decoupling: it separates DNS functionality from the NAT translation itself. The old NAT-PT tried to handle DNS at the same place where addresses were translated, creating dependencies and constraints. Stateful 64 allows a DNS64 function to synthesize IPv6 addresses independently, as long as the synthesized addresses follow the RFC 6052 format. This architectural change avoids many of the topology and DNS-related problems that plagued NAT-PT.

Additionally, stateful 64 is narrower in scope than NAT-PT. It explicitly focuses on IPv6-only clients reaching IPv4-only servers (Scenarios 1 and 5 in RFC 6144), not the reverse. This narrower scope means some problems simply do not apply.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big translator doing everything, the new system splits the work: one part handles addresses, another handles DNS. Splitting them up avoids some of the old system's mistakes.

sections.title: Problems and Solutions
sections.content:
The analysis organizes the 16 concerns from RFC 4966 into three categories:

Impossible to solve: Three issues are fundamental to the problem of translation, not specific to NAT-PT or NAT64. Protocols without demultiplexing capabilities cannot be redirected by any NAT. Information loss between IPv4 and IPv6 headers is inherent to the protocol designs. Mobile IPv6 nodes require proxy behavior incompatible with all NAT flavors.

Can be solved: Seven issues can be addressed but require effort. Protocols embedding IP addresses (like FTP) need application layer gateways or client support. SCTP is out of scope. Multicast is not addressed. Scalability, DNS record validity, IPsec tunnel mode, and address selection depend on deployment details or external mechanisms.

Solved: Eight problems have been resolved. Separating DNS from NAT eliminates topology constraints. Fragmentation handling follows NAT recommendations. Inappropriate DNS responses are avoided. DNS-ALG state issues are gone. DNSSEC validation works for clients doing their own synthesis. DoS concerns from DNS state creation are eliminated. NAT64 follows RFC 4787, RFC 5382, and RFC 5508 recommendations, giving applications higher confidence in session lifetimes. Address persistence is ensured by NAT64's address pooling.
sections.eli5: Some problems can never be fixed—they are just how translation works. Some problems need extra effort from applications or networks. And some problems the new system fixed completely. The analysis shows which is which.

sections.title: Shortcomings and Outlook
sections.content:
The analysis reveals that stateful 64 resolves the majority of DNS-ALG-specific problems and several general NAT concerns. However, many unaddressed problems remain. The majority of these unsolved problems are not specific to 64 but are generic limitations of all NAT-based solutions. Addressing them would require significant increases to complexity.

The document concludes that stateful 64 represents progress but with important caveats. IPv6-only to IPv4-only communication works within the defined scope. However, the reverse direction, IPv4 clients to IPv6 servers, is not supported except through static or explicit bindings (such as port control). Real-world deployments must account for the remaining generic NAT limitations: protocols with embedded addresses, multicast, mobility, and address-semantics issues.
sections.eli5: The new system is better than the old one, but it still has limits. Most of the remaining problems are just hard—any translator would face them. Some situations need extra setup.
